fun_facts: Size, not chromosomes, decides who you're looking at in a school of big white marlin: virtually every fish over about 6.5 feet long is female, because males stop growing well before they reach that length.

White marlin have a near-identical twin: the roundscale spearfish wasn't confirmed as a distinct species until genetic testing in 2006, and a later DNA survey found that roughly 1 in 6 fish anglers had logged as "white marlin" in the western Atlantic were actually roundscale spearfish.

White marlin were among the very first billfish tagged when the US's oldest fish-tagging program broadened from tuna to billfish in the early 1970s; the tag-and-release ethic anglers practice on this species today traces directly back to that research effort.

measures.label: Lower jaw fork length
measures.help: Tip of the lower jaw to the fork of the tail, measured in a straight line -- the standard billfish measurement.

vocabs.label: Sex
vocabs.help: White marlin cannot be sexed externally in the field; unknown is the normal answer.

vocabs.label: Condition at release
vocabs.help: Billfish tagging is normally done boat-side, leaving the fish in the water where possible.

not_taggable.reason: a fish in poor condition or bleeding is unlikely to survive release, so tagging it wastes the tag and the reward

must_release.reason: Atlantic white marlin may legally be retained only by an angler holding a federal Highly Migratory Species permit landing a fish at or above a 66-inch lower jaw fork length minimum, counted against that same national quota of 250 marlin and spearfish landed per year; every white marlin encountered in this tagging programme is released
